This control reads the AIX directed_broadcast network setting to confirm the server drops directed broadcast packets. If directed broadcasts are accepted, an attacker can send them with a forged source address and have the server bounce them in bulk to the spoofed target, using this machine to amplify a flood aimed at someone else.

This control checks whether the server answers ICMP address mask requests, which reveal the subnet mask of its local network to anyone who asks. A server that sends these replies makes it easier for an attacker to map the network and plan further attacks. Leaving this enabled exposes network structure that should stay private.

This check confirms the system does not answer ICMP timestamp requests, which would reveal its exact current time to anyone who asks. If the system does answer them, an attacker can learn the clock time and use it to defeat time-based protections such as login codes and replay windows, or to time attacks across systems. The check passes when the icmptimestamp network setting is 0, meaning timestamp replies are turned off.

The AIX host has a network setting, ip6srcrouteforward, that controls whether it forwards source-routed IPv6 packets. If the setting is not zero, an attacker can write a route into a packet and steer that traffic around firewalls and routing rules to reach systems that should be unreachable from the outside.

This control checks whether the host ignores ICMP redirect messages rather than using them to update its routing table. If the host accepts these messages, an attacker who can send one can silently rewrite the routing table and steer traffic to a machine they control, enabling interception or denial of service.

This check verifies that the AIX network option ipsendredirects is turned off so the system does not send ICMP redirect messages that tell other hosts to change their route. Redirect messages should come only from routers; a regular host that emits them leaks its view of the network and can be used to steer traffic toward a machine an attacker controls, allowing traffic to be redirected or intercepted.

This control checks that the AIX network setting ipsrcrouteforward is off, so the host will not forward IP packets that carry a source-route header. Source-routed packets let the sender choose the path traffic takes, so if forwarding is on an attacker can steer traffic around firewalls and reach parts of the network that should be off-limits.

Source-routed IP packets carry instructions telling the network which path they must take. This check verifies the system is set to reject such packets rather than accept them. If it accepts them, an attacker can force traffic along a route they control, bypassing firewall rules and routing policy.

This control checks that the server is configured not to send source-routed packets, where the sender writes the route a packet takes into the packet itself. If sending source-routed packets is enabled, an attacker can dictate the return path of traffic, steering it around firewalls and routing controls.

This control checks that AIX is configured so NFS clients use privileged reserved ports when they connect to NFS servers. NFS servers treat the source port as a weak form of authentication, so a client connecting from an ordinary unprivileged port is easier to impersonate. If the setting is off, NFS clients may use unprivileged ports, letting an attacker spoof NFS traffic that a server may wrongly trust.

This check confirms the AIX setting that controls whether the system accepts source-routed packets sent to other machines is turned off. Source routing lets whoever sends a packet choose the path it takes across the network. If the setting is left on, an attacker can steer traffic around firewalls and other network controls so it reaches systems that should be unreachable.

AIX limits how much of its network memory pool can be in use before it starts refusing new sockets, and sockthresh is the setting that holds that limit. This check reads the current value and expects a hardened one well below the level AIX ships with, rather than the stock setting. A limit left at or near the shipped level lets a runaway or hostile process consume the network memory pool and leave other services unable to open connections.

This control checks that AIX TCP path-MTU discovery is disabled, as required by the baseline. When the setting is left on, the system keeps per-connection packet-size state based on ICMP traffic, which an attacker on an untrusted network can abuse to stall or break connections and cause a denial of service. A failed check means the system remains open to that attack.

This control checks that the AIX tcp_tcpsecure network setting is fully turned on. When enabled, the setting blocks forged TCP packets from resetting or hijacking a connection that is already in progress. If it is off, an attacker could send a forged packet to knock a live session offline or inject data into it, causing outages and tampering with in-flight traffic.

This control checks that the udp_pmtu_discover network setting is turned off (value 0). That setting controls UDP path-MTU discovery, which keeps per-path state driven by ICMP messages. If it is left on, an attacker on an untrusted network can abuse that state to cause a denial of service.

This check compares how many network services are listening on addresses reachable from the network against whether AIX IP Security packet filtering is active on the host. Every listening service is a door into the system from the network. When services are reachable and the host has no active packet filter, the machine depends entirely on the upstream firewall, so one misrouted subnet or changed rule can expose every one of those services at once.

This control inventories the network configuration of the server: which interfaces exist, the IP addresses assigned to them, the default route used to reach other networks, and the DNS name servers the system queries. It reports an inventory rather than a pass or fail, and without a site-approved baseline it is recorded as not assessed. If this information cannot be collected or compared against an expected state, a missing, unexpected, or wrongly configured interface, route, or resolver could go unnoticed and traffic or name lookups could be misdirected.

This control verifies that every NFS share this system mounts from a remote server has the nosuid and nodev options set. If nosuid is missing, a program planted on the remote share can run with elevated privileges on this system; if nodev is missing, device files on the share are treated as local devices. Either condition lets a compromised or hostile file server gain more access than a shared directory should allow.

This control checks whether the server is configured to mount remote file systems over NFS, as recorded in the /etc/filesystems file. If any such NFS client mount is still configured, the server will connect to a remote system and treat its files as if they were local. An attacker who controls that remote system could use the mount to plant programs that run with administrator privileges, which can lead to full system compromise.

This check reads the local active NFS export table and fails when any exported directory lacks an explicit client access allow list. An unrestricted export can be mounted by any system that can reach it, exposing its files to unauthorized reading or modification.

This control checks that every directory this server shares over NFS is configured to require some form of authentication. It flags any share that declares no security setting at all, or one that explicitly allows the no-authentication option known as none. If it fails, someone who can reach the server over the network could mount that shared directory without proving who they are and read or change its contents.

This control reviews the NFS export rules in the /etc/exports file and the list of filesystems currently being exported, looking for exports that give root authority to anonymous or broadly defined clients, or that allow write access without limiting which clients may connect. A failing export lets any client that can reach the NFS service read and change the exported files as root, so an attacker could view or alter data without needing a valid account.

This control checks the NFS export configuration file /etc/exports to confirm that no export grants access to a client named localhost, 127.0.0.1, or ::1. Because a remote host can claim these loopback names for itself, an export that trusts them can be mounted over the network by a machine the administrator never authorized, exposing the shared directory and the data in it.

This control checks the rcnfs boot entry that controls whether the NFS file-sharing service starts automatically when the system boots. A machine that does not need to share files should not be running NFS; if this entry is present, the system boots into a file-sharing service that an attacker can probe and, where its settings are weak, use to reach files on the host. DISA STIG V-215352 states the rule as a prohibition: running "lsitab rcnfs" must yield no output at all, so the check fails whenever any rcnfs record exists in /etc/inittab.

This control checks whether the host has the NFS file-sharing server installed (the bos.net.nfs.server package). NFS lets a system share its filesystems with other computers over the network, so a host with this server can serve its files to network clients. When that server exists on a system that does not need to export files, there is a real risk that its data gets shared with machines that should not have access to it.

Detects whether an AIX box is a NIM client and names its NIM master. On a NIM-managed LPAR the mksysb and lpp_source restore images normally live on the master, so a thin local backup story is expected — this check confirms the OS restore point is centralized there and tells you which master to verify.

This control checks whether the Network Installation Management (NIM) master software package is installed on the system. A NIM master is a privileged server that can push operating system installs and run commands on the other AIX systems it manages. If one is present where it is not intended, taking over that system gives an attacker a ready-made way to control every machine it manages.

This control confirms that the Network Information Service (NIS) client software is not installed on the system. NIS is a legacy directory service that shares account and password information across the network with little protection, so a system running the NIS client can have its login credentials exposed or be made to trust a malicious NIS server that an attacker controls.

This control checks the password and group files (/etc/passwd and /etc/group) for any line that begins with a plus sign. A leading plus turns on a legacy network directory feature called NIS, so this machine will accept users and groups served from the network instead of only the ones defined locally. If that entry is present, anyone who can control or impersonate that network directory could add accounts, including privileged ones, and use them to log in to this system.

This control checks whether the NIS server software package bos.net.nis.server is installed on the system. NIS is a legacy network authentication service that stores account names and password hashes and answers queries from other machines, and a modern system rarely needs one. If the package is present, a NIS server could be answering those queries over the network, letting an attacker harvest usernames and password hashes or feed false data to systems that trust the server.

This check reads virtual FC (NPIV) mappings with ioscli lsmap -all -npiv and reports vfchost adapters that are not logged in to the fabric. No vfchost on a confirmed VIOS is not applicable. A failed lsmap is not assessed. The check never changes a mapping.

This check judges whether the NPIV paths on a VIOS are actually redundant: a vfchost that is not logged in is a dead path, and vfchosts that all ride one physical FC adapter are a single point of failure. No vfchost on a confirmed VIOS is not applicable. A failed lsmap is not assessed. The check never changes a mapping.

This control checks that the host keeps its clock synchronized using the Network Time Protocol (NTP). A compliant host has the NTP daemon active, at least one time server configured in /etc/ntp.conf, and an NTP poll interval bound (maxpoll) of 16 (about 18 hours) or less so the clock is disciplined at least every 24 hours. When time sync is missing, too sparsely polled, or the clock drifts, log timestamps become unreliable and time-sensitive security features such as Kerberos and TLS can fail.

This check confirms that the AIX release is still inside the IBM standard support window, so it keeps receiving security fixes. A release past its end-of-support date no longer gets IBM security fixes, leaving newly disclosed CVEs open on the host; the check flags it for upgrade to a supported release, with a Software Support Service Extension only as a bridge. On a VIOS, or when not running as root, the check does not assess and reports NOT_ASSESSED.

This check confirms the AIX (or VIOS) Technology Level is current for its release and still inside its service-pack fix-support window. A box that lags the release latest Technology Level, or whose TL has passed its fix-support end date, is no longer receiving the defect and security fixes IBM publishes for the current TL, so newly disclosed CVEs can remain open. On a VIOS the underlying AIX level is a secondary signal behind the VIOS level.

This control measures how full the paging space of the system is. Paging space is the disk overflow used when physical memory runs short. If it fills up, the system can no longer allocate memory to running programs and will start killing them, and heavy use in the meantime means the machine is swapping to disk and running slowly.

This check detects whether the system is actively paging memory to and from disk. Paging means the system has run out of real memory and is moving pages out to disk and reading them back, which adds disk latency to every memory access. When paging is sustained, the whole system slows down.

This check reviews where a system keeps its paging space, the disk area used when memory runs low. If several paging spaces share one physical disk, or all paging space sits in the system volume group while other disks are available, the disk becomes a single point of contention and cannot work in parallel. Under heavy memory demand the system can slow sharply or stop responding, interrupting service.

This control checks that every AIX paging space is active and the same size, so the system spreads memory paging evenly across all of them. If one space is smaller or inactive, paging piles onto the remaining spaces and the system can run short of usable paging capacity and slow or stop under memory load, even when total paging space looks sufficient.

Checks how old the installed AIX operating system build is, using the build week the operating system reports. An old build is missing years of security and stability fixes, which leaves the system exposed to known attacks and reliability problems.

This check looks at the running system for signs that the memory buffers AIX uses to move data to disk and paging space have run out since the last boot. When those buffers run dry, disk I/O and paging stall, which can slow every process on the box. A healthy box has never hit these limits; a box that has hit them was under real memory pressure.

AIX records system performance over time using a background collector such as topasrec, nmon, or njmon. This check confirms that at least one of those collectors is actively running. If none is running, no performance history is being saved, leaving capacity planning and the investigation of past slowdowns or outages to guesswork.

This check looks at the running service inventory to see whether the piobe print subsystem is active. piobe is the AIX print job backend and is often left running on servers that never print. Any subsystem left active is more privileged code running, more to patch and monitor, and more attack surface than the business asked for on a machine with no printing role.

This check reports the state of the PowerHA (HACMP) high-availability cluster on an AIX system, but only when the PowerHA cluster filesets are actually installed. A cluster that is not in the ST_STABLE state cannot fail over, so the standby node that is supposed to take over when a node dies will not, and the outage the cluster exists to prevent is exactly what happens.

commands: lssec -f /etc/security/user -s root -a rlogin -a sugroups -a admin -a expires
checks.blurb: This check confirms that the root account on an AIX system is locked down: root cannot sign in directly over the network, and only a named administrator group may switch to the root user. If either gate is left open, anyone who guesses or steals the root password could take over the entire system, with no record of who did it.

This check watches maxuproc, the AIX ceiling on how many processes one account may run at the same time. It compares the highest per-account process count against that ceiling and warns as the limit is approached. When the ceiling is reached, new processes cannot start, so applications and shells fail to spawn work.

This check confirms that no account in the system password file (/etc/security/passwd) has a blank password. An account with a blank password lets anyone sign in to it without entering a credential. If the check fails, an attacker who can reach the system login can take over that account and everything it is allowed to do.

This control checks that the default password policy points to a dictionary of common words, so AIX rejects them when a user chooses a new password. If no dictionary is set, or the setting is malformed, users can pick easy-to-guess passwords such as password or welcome, which are the first words an attacker tries, making accounts much quicker to break into.

This control checks that the system is configured to hash passwords with a Loadable Password Algorithm, either ssha512 or ssha256, instead of the legacy DES crypt default. If it fails, stored passwords are protected only by the old DES method, which ignores everything past the eighth character. An attacker who obtains the password file can then crack even long passwords far more quickly.

This control checks how many weeks must pass before a previously used password can be used again, a reuse window stored in the histexpire attribute of the /etc/security/user file. It expects that window to be at least fifty-two weeks. If the window is missing or too short, someone who already knows an older password can reuse it almost as soon as the account changes to a new one, defeating the benefit of password rotation.

This control checks that the AIX default password policy prevents users from reusing recent passwords. It reads the password history setting in the /etc/security/user file, which must keep the last 20 to 50 passwords out of reuse. If that history is missing, too small, or switched off, a user can cycle back to a password that was already exposed, so forced password changes give no real protection.

This control checks the failed-login limit in the default AIX account settings, the loginretries attribute in the file /etc/security/user. A low limit locks an account after a few wrong passwords, which stops an attacker from trying thousands of guesses until one works. If the limit is missing or set too high, an attacker can keep guessing a password and eventually take over the account.

This control checks the default password expiry setting (maxage) in the /etc/security/user file, which sets how long a password stays valid before it must be changed. If that value is set to zero or beyond the approved limit, passwords never expire or stay usable far too long, so a stolen password keeps working until it is discovered and changed by hand.

This control checks the default password maximum age setting in the /etc/security/user file and requires it to be between 1 and 52 weeks. A setting of zero disables password expiry, so a stolen or guessed password remains usable indefinitely. A value above 52 weeks keeps passwords valid for more than a year, giving an attacker that much longer to use a compromised account.

This control checks the default AIX password settings to confirm that a password, once it reaches its expiry date, can be changed by its holder for only a short capped window before an administrator must reset it. If that window is set to unlimited, or password expiry is switched off, an old or stolen password never forces a reset and an attacker who has one can keep control of the account indefinitely.

This control checks the AIX maxrepeats password setting, which caps how many times a single character may be repeated in a new password. If repeats are not tightly limited, users can set passwords built mostly from one repeated character, and attackers can guess those weak passwords much faster and take over the accounts.

This control checks the default maxulogs setting in /etc/security/user, which limits how many login sessions a single account may hold open at the same time. If that limit is missing or set above ten, one account can be signed in from many places at once, so a stolen password could be used in parallel without the real user being logged out. Session records then cannot show how many people are actually sharing the account.

This control checks the AIX minimum password age setting (minage) on the default user account. That setting imposes a waiting period before a password can be changed again, which stops a user from immediately cycling back to a previously used or weak password. If it is zero, a user can change a password over and over in one sitting and bypass the password history and forced-change rules.

This control checks the AIX password policy setting that requires a minimum number of letters in new passwords. If the setting is missing or set too low, users can pick passwords with few or no letters, like a phone number or date. Those are easy for an attacker to guess, letting them log into accounts on the system directly, with no technical exploit needed.

This check verifies that a new password must differ from the previous password by at least six characters. If that rule is missing or set too low, someone can change a password while keeping nearly all of the old one. Anyone who already knew the old password could then guess the replacement with little effort, so the change provides no real protection.

This control checks the AIX password rule that sets the minimum number of digits every new password must contain. If the rule is unset or set to zero, users can choose passwords with no digits at all, making them easier to guess or crack and leaving accounts open to compromise.

This control checks the system-wide password policy that sets a minimum length for every new password. It reads that setting for the default account in the file /etc/security/user and expects at least 14 characters. If it fails, users who inherit the default policy can pick very short or empty passwords, which are easy to guess or crack and let an attacker sign in as that user.

This check reads the minloweralpha password setting from the system default policy to confirm that every new password must include at least one lower-case letter. If the setting is missing or zero, accounts can be given passwords with no lower-case letters, which narrows the range of passwords an attacker has to try and makes them easier to guess.

This control checks the minother setting in the AIX default password rules, which requires each password to contain a minimum number of non-alphabetic characters such as digits or symbols. It passes when that minimum is between three and eight. If the setting is missing, too low, or outside the valid range, passwords may be made up almost entirely of letters, which attackers can guess or crack much faster.

This control checks the AIX password policy setting that decides how many special characters, such as symbols or punctuation, every new password must contain. If the setting is not enforced, users can create passwords made only of letters and numbers, which are much easier for an attacker to guess or crack. That leaves accounts vulnerable to unauthorized access.

This check confirms that the system password policy requires every new password to contain at least one upper-case letter, using the minupperalpha setting in the default user profile. If that requirement is absent or set to zero, new passwords may contain no upper-case letters at all, making them easier for an attacker to guess or crack.

commands: awk '/^[^ \t:][^:]*:[ \t]*$/ { u=$1; sub(/:[ \t]*$/,"",u); n++ } $1=="flags" && $2=="=" && $0 ~ /NOCHECK/ && u!="" { k++; if (k<=6) users=(users=="")?u:users","u } END { printf "scanned=%d nocheck=%d users=%s\n", n, k, users }' /etc/security/passwd
checks.blurb: This control checks whether any account is exempt from password strength and history rules because of the NOCHECK flag in the AIX password database. An account with this flag can be given a weak or previously used password, which gives an attacker a much easier way to break in through a normal login.

commands: lssec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a maxage -a minlen -a loginretries -a histsize
checks.blurb: This check reads the default password rules that every new account on the system inherits: how long a password stays valid, its minimum length, how many failed logins are allowed, and how many old passwords are remembered. If those defaults are weak, each account created afterwards starts out weak too, which makes passwords easier to guess or reuse and the system easier to break into.

commands: awk '/^[^ \t:][^:]*:[ \t]*$/ { u=$1; sub(/:[ \t]*$/,"",u); n++ } $1=="password" && $2=="=" && NF==3 && length($3)==13 && u!="" && u !~ /^(adm|bin|daemon|invscout|ipsec|lp|lpd|nobody|nuucp|sshd|sys|uucp|esa|srvproxy|imnadm|anonymou|ftp)$/ { k++; if (k<=6) users=(users=="")?u:users","u } END { printf "scanned=%d crypt=%d users=%s\n", n, k, users }' /etc/security/passwd
checks.blurb: This control checks /etc/security/passwd for user accounts whose stored password is still protected by the old crypt method, a weak 56-bit algorithm that is easy to crack. If any non-system account still uses it, an attacker who obtains the stored hashes can quickly recover the real passwords and log in as those users. The check reports the affected account names.

This control checks whether the qdaemon print spooler service is active on the system. qdaemon processes queued print jobs, and running it when printing is not needed leaves an unnecessary service live that adds to the code an attacker can target. If the check fails, that avoidable service exposure is present without a business need to offset it.

This control verifies that the IPv6 autoconfiguration service is set to start automatically from the TCP/IP startup file /etc/rc.tcpip at every boot. If that startup entry is missing, the server will not configure its IPv6 addresses on its own, so IPv6 network services can fail after a reboot or when the network changes.

This control checks whether the DHCP client service is running on the server or set to start at boot. Servers should hold a fixed address, but a running DHCP client accepts its IP address, gateway, and name servers from any DHCP server that responds on the network. If this fails, an attacker who places a rogue DHCP server on the network could point the system at hostile settings and redirect its traffic, or the address could change and break connectivity.

This check confirms the DHCP relay service (dhcprd) is not running on the system. dhcprd forwards address requests between networks, so it should only be enabled on a server that is meant to act as a relay. If it runs where it is not needed, an attacker who can reach it could feed clients false network settings, such as a wrong gateway or name server, to redirect their traffic or intercept it.

This check confirms the system is not running a DHCP server service (dhcpsd), either now or set to start at boot. A server that unexpectedly hands out IP addresses and network settings can let an attacker redirect traffic from other machines, or hand out conflicting addresses that break the network.

This control checks whether the gated routing service is set to start at boot in /etc/rc.tcpip or is currently running as a system service. The gated service provides legacy network routing protocols (RIP, OSPF, and BGP) and has no legitimate purpose on a server that is not a network router. If it is running where it should not be, it can advertise or redirect routes on the network, hijacking or disrupting traffic, and it exposes an unneeded legacy service to attack.

This control checks whether the hostmibd service is enabled at boot or running now. hostmibd is a helper that answers SNMP queries about the hardware and software of the machine, and most systems never use it. When it is left on unnecessarily, it is an extra network service an attacker could query for details about the host or probe for weaknesses.

The internet super-server (inetd) is a legacy daemon that listens on many network ports and starts older services such as telnet, FTP, and remote shell on demand. This check identifies systems where inetd is still started at boot from /etc/rc.tcpip or running as an active subsystem. Leaving it enabled when no inetd-managed service is actually required keeps unused ports listening and can let an attacker reach older, unencrypted services that bypass normal access controls.

This check verifies that the mrouted multicast routing daemon is not enabled, either as a start line in the /etc/rc.tcpip boot file or as a running subsystem. mrouted provides multicast routing that a normal server does not need. If it is left running, the system exposes an extra network service that an attacker can target, widening the ways into the system for no benefit.

This check verifies that the named DNS server service is not running on the server. It checks whether named is set to start from the boot configuration file /etc/rc.tcpip or is already active as a system service. If named runs on a server that is not meant to be a DNS server, it leaves an unmanaged DNS service answering queries on the network, which attackers can abuse to reflect and amplify traffic or probe for a way in.

This check confirms that the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery daemon, ndpd-host, is set to start at boot by looking for its start entry in the /etc/rc.tcpip startup file. ndpd-host plays the role for IPv6 that ARP plays for IPv4: it finds neighboring devices, keeps the neighbor cache current, and learns about local routers. If the start entry is missing, the daemon does not run after a reboot, and IPv6 traffic can fail because the host cannot reach neighbors or find a route off its own network.

This control checks the boot file /etc/rc.tcpip to confirm the IPv6 router service (ndpd-router) is disabled, so the machine will not start acting as an IPv6 router when it boots. If this fails, the machine could come up advertising itself as a router and forwarding IPv6 traffic, which lets an attacker redirect or intercept that traffic or knock IPv6 connectivity offline on the network.

This control checks whether the portmap service, the RPC port mapper, is running on the system. It flags portmap when it is set to start at boot in the file /etc/rc.tcpip or is already active as a running service. If portmap runs while nothing on the system genuinely needs RPC, it gives a remote attacker a live list of the services and port numbers to attack, plus a well-known network service with a long history of security flaws.

This control checks whether the legacy routed service is running, either started at boot from /etc/rc.tcpip or active in the service inventory. Routed maintains routing tables using the old RIP1 protocol, which accepts updates from anyone on the network without authentication. If it is left enabled, an attacker could feed it bogus routes to redirect or disrupt traffic on this host.

This check confirms the rwhod service is not in use, meaning it is not started at boot from /etc/rc.tcpip and not running as an active system service. rwhod is a legacy daemon that broadcasts the names of logged-in users across the network, which is rarely needed and lets anyone on the wire see who is using the system. A failure means the server is running that service, leaking login information and exposing an extra network service that attackers can probe.

This control confirms that the sendmail mail service is not in use, by checking that it is not started at boot in /etc/rc.tcpip and not running as a service. Sendmail is an older mail daemon with a long history of remotely exploitable vulnerabilities, so leaving it running on a server that does not handle mail exposes an unnecessary, attackable network service. If this control fails, an attacker who can reach that open port may be able to exploit a known sendmail flaw to run code or gain privileged access.

This control checks whether the obsolete timed network service is running, either started at boot from the /etc/rc.tcpip file or active as a running system service. timed provides a legacy UNIX time service that has been replaced by NTP. Leaving it running exposes an outdated and unnecessary network service that widens the attack surface and can give any system that still connects to it unreliable time.

This control verifies that the legacy r-command filesets bos.net.tcp.rcmd and bos.net.tcp.rcmd_server are either not installed or have every owned file stripped of all read, write, and execute permissions. These r-command tools let one host run commands and copy files on another using host-based trust instead of a user password, and they send all traffic in clear text. If the filesets remain installed and usable, anyone who can reach the network could run commands or copy files on remote systems without credentials, and passwords or data in transit could be captured.

This control checks that system logging is set up to forward a copy of its records to a remote server, shown by an @ entry in the /etc/syslog.conf file. Forwarding keeps an independent copy of the logs so they survive a crash, disk failure, or an attack on the host itself. If no remote target is set, the only copy of the logs lives on the machine that produced them, so an attacker who takes it over can wipe the evidence and a hardware failure destroys the record of what happened.

This check scans the whole local filesystem tree from / for files named .netrc. A .netrc file stores a remote host, an account name and the password of that account in plain text so that ftp and rexec can log in without an interactive password exchange. Anyone who can read the file (its owner, root, a backup copy, or an attacker who gains any foothold on the host) obtains working credentials for the remote systems it names and can reuse them elsewhere. Any .netrc file anywhere on the system is a finding.

This control checks the file /etc/hosts.equiv for active trust entries. A host named in that file is trusted to connect to this system and sign in to matching local accounts without a password. If the check fails, an attacker who compromises one of the trusted hosts, or anyone with an account on it, can reach this system as a local user without any password.

The .rhosts, .shosts, hosts.equiv and shosts.equiv files list hosts that are trusted to log in without a password. If any of them is present anywhere on the system, anyone who compromises one of those hosts can move laterally onto this system with no password check.

This check confirms that the Resource Monitoring and Control path the HMC uses for DLPAR and partition management is active on a VIOS. It reads the ctrmc SRC subsystem and rmcdomainstatus. If ctrmc is not active or no HMC management-domain control point is Up, the HMC cannot drive DLPAR, LPM, or concurrent firmware activation on this VIOS. On a plain AIX LPAR the VIOS appliance form of this check does not apply.

rootvg is the volume group that holds the AIX operating system. Mirroring it keeps a second copy of every operating-system file on another disk, so the server keeps running if one disk fails. A rootvg that is unmirrored, partially mirrored, or running with a stale or missing mirror copy is a single disk failure away from a full outage.

This check confirms whether quorum is enabled on a fully-mirrored rootvg. On a 2-disk mirror, QUORUM=2 can keep the surviving disk from varying on at boot after a disk failure, so most shops disable it (chvg -Qn rootvg). Reports PASS when quorum is disabled, WARN when it is enabled, and NOT_APPLICABLE when rootvg is not a full mirror.

This check confirms that every online, non-rootvg volume group has a recent local savevg backup. A rootvg (mksysb) backup restores the operating system but not application data, so each data volume group needs its own savevg image under /tmp/vgdata/<VG>. A volume group with no recent savevg evidence has no known restore point for its application data.

This check verifies that every Shared Ethernet Adapter on a VIOS is configured to fail over to its partner VIOS: ha_mode is auto, standby, or sharing, a control channel (or a CAA cluster) is in place to arbitrate the primary/backup roles, and each side has a priority. Without that, one VIOS is a single point of failure for every client LPAR bridged through its SEA — when it goes down, the network goes down with it.

This check reads the Shared Ethernet Adapter largesend attribute on a VIOS. IBM documents 0 as disabled and 1 as enabled, and says largesend should be enabled on the SEA when the physical adapter has large send enabled (https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/how-determine-if-large-send-offload-lsolargesend-and-large-receive-offload-lrolargereceive-are-enabled-sea and https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/seaproc-consuming-high-cpu-vios). The physical adapter is not visible from the SEA attribute alone, so 0 is a warning rather than a failure. No SEA is not applicable. The check never runs chdev.

This check records the Shared Ethernet Adapter thread attribute on a VIOS. IBM does not require thread=1. https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/ibm-virtual-io-server-download-support says thread=1 is the default after APAR IY62264 and thread=0 is a valid throughput choice (more consistent quality of service, lower LAN throughput). Either value passes. The check does not invent a required setting and never runs chdev. No SEA is not applicable.

This check confirms that the tracked security APARs for the technology level are installed, credited either to a Service Pack (instfix -ik) or to an installed interim fix (emgr -lv3). A tracked APAR missing from both means the box is still exposed to a published, fixed vulnerability (CVE-2025-36250, NIM nimesis remote command execution) whose fix is available but not applied.

This check confirms whether AIX was installed using the Secure by Default option, which installs a minimal software set and leaves out remote-access programs such as telnet and ftp that send passwords across the network as readable text. If that option was not selected at installation, those programs can be present and reachable, so anyone able to read network traffic could capture login passwords, and services such as rsh, rcp and sendmail add extra remote-access points an attacker can probe.

This control verifies that the SMTP greeting offered by sendmail does not disclose the sendmail version. The SmtpGreetingMessage parameter in /etc/mail/sendmail.cf must not contain the $v or $Z macros; a greeting that expands those macros reveals the exact sendmail version to any connecting client, giving an attacker the information needed to target version-specific weaknesses.

This control verifies the sendmail PrivacyOptions setting in /etc/mail/sendmail.cf contains the goaway keyword, which disables the SMTP EXPN and VRFY features (among others). With EXPN or VRFY active, anyone can ask the mail server whether an address or mailing list exists and harvest valid addresses for spam or targeted attacks.

An interactive shell session can keep running until someone closes it. This check verifies that /etc/profile sets both TMOUT and TIMEOUT to 600 seconds or less, uncommented, so an idle login session is terminated after 10 minutes of inactivity (DISA STIG V-215320). Without it, an unattended session stays open and anyone who reaches it can act with the full privileges of that account.

This control checks that idle shell sessions on the system are configured to log themselves out automatically. It confirms the /etc/profile startup file sets both TMOUT and TIMEOUT to a value between 1 and 900 seconds and marks them readonly, so a user cannot change or remove the timeout. If these settings are missing or can be edited, a session left open at an unattended terminal stays logged in indefinitely, letting anyone with access to the screen or the machine take over an already-authenticated login.

This control checks whether the AIX network analysis package bos.net.snapp is installed on the server. It is a specialized diagnostic tool that most production systems do not need. If it is present, anyone who gains access to the server has a ready-made way to observe network traffic, and the system carries an extra rarely used package that adds attack surface.

SNMP lets remote management tools read and write information about a system over the network. SNMP community strings are the password that controls this access, and many systems ship with a well-known default such as public or private. The STIG also flags any uncommented default-password token (smux peer password, private, and similar) in the SNMP configuration. If one of these defaults is still in use, anyone who can reach the box on the network can read, or even modify, its SNMP data.

This control checks that the SNMP network-management software is not installed on the system. It fails if the SNMP client or server package is present in the package inventory. SNMP often runs with well-known default community passwords and sends data without encryption, so an installed copy can give a network attacker a way to read system details or change settings.

This control checks whether the system has a trustworthy record of the software installed on it, which is the starting point for knowing what needs patching or replacing. If that record is missing, incomplete, or cannot be trusted, programs on the system can go unaccounted for, and outdated or unsupported software may remain in place with no one checking it for missing fixes or known flaws.

This control checks that the SSH service is configured with an allow list or deny list of users or groups (AllowUsers, AllowGroups, DenyUsers, or DenyGroups). When none of these is set, the server accepts remote login attempts for every account that has a working password or key, so a single weak or leaked credential opens a way in.

This control checks that the SSH service is set to display a warning message before anyone can log in, and that the message file actually exists. If no banner is shown, people connecting over SSH get no advance notice that the system is monitored and restricted to authorized use, which removes a simple deterrent and weakens the legal footing for holding an intruder accountable.

This check reads the effective SSH cipher list and confirms the server offers only strong, modern ciphers. If the server still offers broken or deprecated ciphers such as CBC, arcfour, 3DES, or Blowfish, an attacker watching the connection may be able to downgrade the session to a weak cipher and decrypt traffic that looked secure.

SSH sessions that sit idle too long can leave an open doorway into the system if the user walks away from a logged-in terminal. This control checks the SSH server idle-session timeout settings, ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax, to confirm abandoned sessions are automatically disconnected within fifteen minutes. If they are not, an unattended session can be hijacked by anyone who reaches that machine, and stale connections keep consuming system resources.

This check confirms the system has no host-based trust database, meaning neither /etc/rhosts.equiv nor /etc/shosts.equiv exists. When one of these files is present, a remote host named in it is trusted to access accounts on this system without a password. An attacker who controls that trusted host could then log in here without any credential, bypassing normal authentication.

SSH can be configured to trust a connection based on the machine it comes from, through host-based authentication or rhosts files, instead of checking the credentials that belong to the account being logged into. This check verifies that the SSH server has IgnoreRhosts set to yes and HostbasedAuthentication set to no, so every login must prove its own identity. If either setting is wrong, someone who gains access to one trusted machine, or who can plant an rhosts entry, could log in to other accounts without supplying the password or key for those accounts.

This control checks which key-exchange algorithms the SSH server will accept, flagging the server if any of three deprecated SHA-1 based algorithms are still enabled. Key exchange is the handshake that sets up the encryption for every SSH session, and these older algorithms use cryptography that attackers can now break. If the check fails, an attacker who can observe or intercept a connection may be able to defeat that encryption and read the session, including logins and any data transferred.

This control checks the LoginGraceTime setting on the SSH server, which is the number of seconds an unauthenticated connection may stay open while a user completes login. It passes only when that window is between 1 and 60 seconds. If the window is disabled or too long, an attacker can hold many half-open connections to exhaust the server and block legitimate users from logging in.

This control checks the logging level of SSH, the service that allows remote login to the system. SSH must be set to INFO or VERBOSE so that login attempts and authentication failures are written to the security log. If the level is set too low, break-in attempts go unrecorded and an attacker leaves no trace; if it is set to DEBUG, the logs can fill with sensitive detail about accounts and sessions that should not be exposed.

This check confirms the SSH server allows only approved message authentication (MAC) algorithms, which guard against tampering with data sent over an SSH connection. If an unapproved algorithm is enabled, an attacker able to intercept the connection could alter or forge transmitted data without being detected.

SSH MaxAuthTries limits how many login attempts a single SSH connection is allowed before the server closes it, and this check confirms that limit is four or fewer. If the limit is set higher, an attacker who reaches the SSH service can make many password guesses per connection before being cut off, which makes brute-force password guessing faster and more likely to succeed.

This control verifies that the OpenSSH client and server software packages are both installed and healthy. OpenSSH is what provides encrypted remote logins and file transfers to and from the system. If either package is missing or damaged, administrators may lose secure remote access, and connections could fall back to unencrypted protocols that expose passwords and data to anyone watching the network.

This control verifies that the SSH service rejects logins from accounts with no password. It checks the effective PermitEmptyPasswords setting in the SSH server configuration. If empty passwords are allowed, any account left without a password can be logged into over the network with no credentials at all.

This control checks the SSH server setting that determines whether a user can log in directly as root over the network. Root is the account with full control over the system, so if direct root login is not refused, anyone who steals or guesses the root password can connect remotely and take over the machine. Failing this check means the system allows or leaves unspecified direct root login rather than refusing it.

This control checks the SSH server setting PermitUserEnvironment, which decides whether users may bring their own environment variables into a login session. When enabled, a user can supply environment values that the server then applies to programs run in that session. A compromised account could use these values to bypass restrictions in environment-sensitive programs, gaining access or actions the system should not allow.

SSH encrypts each connection with a session key, and the server is meant to negotiate a fresh key so that no single key protects too much traffic. This control reads the effective rekey limit and treats only the exact pairing of 1073741824 bytes and 3600 seconds as meeting the requirement; any other pairing, or none at all, is reported as not meeting it. Where no limit is enforced, one key can cover an entire long-lived session, so an attacker who recovers that key can decrypt far more of the traffic.

This check verifies that direct root login over SSH is disabled on the system. If it is left enabled, the shared root password becomes the single secret an attacker needs for full control, and actions taken as root leave no record of who performed them.

This check confirms the SSH file-transfer subsystem is configured to create uploaded files with a restrictive permission mask and to record transfer activity in the system log. If it is not, files a user uploads can be created with permissions that let other local users read or change them, and file transfers can go unrecorded, leaving misuse undetected.

This control checks that the SSH server is set to verify the ownership and permissions of each user home directory and SSH key files before allowing sign-in. When enabled, the server refuses login for any account whose files are writable by other users. If disabled, someone with access to the server could plant a key in another user account and sign in as that user.

This control checks the version of the SSH server installed on the system and confirms it is OpenSSH major version 9 or newer. Older SSH releases no longer receive current security fixes. A system still running one can be reached by attackers who exploit known weaknesses in that old software to break in or take over the machine.

This control reads the installed OpenSSL and OpenSSH fileset versions on an AIX or VIOS system and flags any OpenSSL release older than the 3.x line. OpenSSL versions before 3.0 have reached the end of upstream support, so a system running them stops receiving current security fixes for its cryptographic stack. If the installed levels cannot be read, the state of that stack is unknown.

This check grades Shared Storage Pool alert thresholds on a VIOS and is separate from ssp_cluster. No cluster is not applicable. After the cluster is present it runs alert -list. PASS only when every ThresholdPercent is an integer from 1 to 99. 35 is the documented default, not the only legal value. No ThresholdPercent line warns. 0, 100, and N/A are not assessed. alert -set is not run.

This check reports the health of the Shared Storage Pool (SSP) / CAA cluster on a VIOS. If a node or the pool reports DOWN, DEGRADED, FAILED or INCOMPLETE, shared storage for the SSP may have lost a redundant path, so it warns. When the cluster and all nodes report OK it passes, and when no cluster is defined it is not applicable.

This check reads Node Upgrade Status from ioscli cluster -status -verbose and is separate from ssp_cluster. No cluster is not applicable. ON_LEVEL passes. UP_LEVEL warns because IBM says that node is not ready for viosupgrade, not because the pool is down. A missing field is not assessed. There is no fail.

This check grades Shared Storage Pool free space on a VIOS and is separate from ssp_cluster. No cluster is not applicable. After the cluster is present it runs lssp -clustername and compares FREE_SPACE with POOL_SIZE. IBM states that I/O operations on the virtual client partition might fail when free space falls below 5 percent of total space. Bare lssp, Size(mb), Free(mb), and rootvg are not graded. 35 percent is the default alert, not this fail-line.

commands: lsuser -a admin maxage account_locked time_last_login ALL
checks.blurb: This check finds privileged accounts, meaning root and any account marked as an administrator, that have not been used in more than 90 days or have never logged in while their password never expires. A dormant account that still holds high privilege is an ideal target for an attacker, because no one notices when a forgotten account gets used, and a password that never expires outlives the person who set it.

checks.question: remote_login_unauthorized_users: Which local user accounts must NOT be able to log in remotely (SSH, rlogin, telnet)? List them, or state that every account currently showing rlogin=true is authorized.
checks.blurb: This check records, for every local account, whether AIX lets that account start an interactive session from the network (the rlogin attribute). An account with rlogin=true can be logged into remotely by anyone who has its password, so an account meant to be console-only or purely non-interactive becomes reachable from the network. AIX itself offers no way to tell an authorized remote user from an unauthorized one, so PTxray only collects the evidence and reports the control as not assessed until the site supplies its own list of accounts that must not log in remotely.
When two accounts share a UID the system cannot tell them apart, so the actions of one user are logged and authorized as those of the other and accountability is lost.

This check looks at /etc/rc.tcpip, the list of network daemons AIX starts at boot, and reports whether aixmibd is still among them. aixmibd is a legacy SNMP MIB sub-agent that most systems no longer need; when it is left enabled it keeps an extra network listener running and answering queries about the machine, which widens the attack surface for no benefit.

Audio input devices such as microphones are readable by whoever their group allows, so an audio device group-owned by an ordinary group lets any member of that group open the device and record what is said near the machine; keeping the group at root, sys, bin or system limits that to administrators.

When the audit bin stanza lacks its trail, bin, backup settings or its size and free-space floors, the audit subsystem can silently stop recording or overwrite records when the audit filesystem fills, destroying the evidence trail.
If AIX does not start auditing at boot, actions taken between boot and any later manual audit start leave no audit trail, so early-boot activity by an intruder is unrecoverable.
This check verifies that audit records have enough room on disk to survive a week. A nearly full audit filesystem can silently drop the evidence needed to reconstruct an incident.

The AIX audit configuration files under /etc/security/audit define what the AIX audit subsystem records. If a non-root account owns one it can edit or truncate that policy and quietly stop events from being recorded, defeating the audit trail.

The configuration files of the audit subsystem under /etc/security/audit must be group-owned by the audit group. When another group owns them, members of that group can edit which events are recorded, so an intruder can switch off the audit trail that would record what they did next.

This check verifies that audit configuration files are not readable or writable beyond root and the audit group. Broader access can let an unprivileged account learn exactly what is being recorded, or alter the audit setup so activity by that same account stops being logged.

The system is supposed to warn while there is still room left in the audit filesystem. If the reserve is set too small, or not set at all, the filesystem fills before anyone is told and the record of what happened stops being written.
Audit logs must be owned by root so their records cannot be edited or truncated by another account. An account that owns an audit log could destroy the evidence of its own activity.

Audit logs record who did what on the system. If a log file is group-owned by a group other than system, members of that group can alter or truncate the record of their own activity, so the audit trail can no longer be trusted as evidence.
Audit trail files record who did what on the system. A mode looser than 660 lets accounts outside root and the audit group read or alter that record, destroying its value as evidence.

This check verifies that the system keeps an audit record of the security-relevant changes the baseline requires. Without a configured audit class applied to every user and without the listed audited objects, the system records no trail of who changed accounts, passwords, groups, limits, or the audit configuration itself, so changes by an intruder go unnoticed.
AIX must produce audit records that carry date, time, and event type information so the audit trail can establish what events occurred.

This check verifies that AIX audit records show the outcome of each audited event. Without a status column, an investigator cannot tell whether a privileged command or login succeeded, so the trail cannot answer what an intruder achieved.

This check verifies that the AIX audit trail records the full text of privileged commands. Without full-text recording, the audit trail can show that a privileged action happened but not exactly what command an administrator or an intruder actually ran, so an investigator cannot reconstruct the action from the record.

This check verifies that AIX audit records contain information establishing where events occurred. It reads the audit trail file named in /etc/security/audit/config and runs auditpr in verbose mode against that log; when event detailed information is displayed, the audit records establish where events occurred. A configured audit trail that auditpr cannot render as detail, or a missing audit trail configuration, is a finding.
Audit records that do not name the user and the process behind an event cannot attribute activity to anyone, so actions by an intruder are indistinguishable from routine work during an investigation.

This check verifies that a role carries the aix.security.audit, aix.security.user.audit, and aix.security.role.audit authorizations. Without such a role, no assigned ISSO or designated SA can change the auditing performed on all operating system components in near real time, as DISA STIG V-215252 requires.
This check verifies that AIX audit logs are rotated daily so trails are archived instead of growing unbounded.

This check verifies that the AIX audit tools under /usr/sbin are owned by the root account. When an audit tool belongs to another account, that account can modify or disable the tool and alter or erase the audit trail, defeating the audit subsystem that records who did what on the system.

This check verifies that the AIX audit tools under /usr/sbin are group-owned by the audit group and that /usr/sbin/auditldap is group-owned by the security group. When those binaries belong to the wrong group, an unauthorized group can access or alter the audit subsystem, so audit evidence can be read, changed, or suppressed.

This check verifies that the AIX audit tools are set to mode 4550 or less and that auditldap is set to mode 500 or less. The audit tools collect, filter and merge audit records, so a group- or other-writable (or otherwise over-permissive) mode lets an unprivileged user alter the audit subsystem and mask activity.
AIX must provide auditselect to filter and reduce audit records on demand (V-215242).
This check verifies that AIX provides /usr/sbin/auditpr so administrators can generate audit reports on demand for review, analysis, and after-the-fact security incident investigation.
AIX must verify the hash of audit tools (trustchk TE/CHKEXEC plus tsd.dat cert_tag/signature/hash_value not VOLATILE for each required audit tool).
This check verifies that the AIX automountd subsystem is not active when automated file system mounting is not required.

This check reads the CDE dtsession saverTimeout and lockTimeout values in each locale sys.resources file on the box. A value above 15 minutes, or a missing timeout, is a finding. An idle CDE session that stays unlocked leaves the console open to anyone who walks up to it.

checks.question: Obtain a list of emergency accounts from the ISSO/ISSM.
checks.blurb: Emergency accounts must be removed or disabled after the crisis is resolved or within 72 hours.

This check runs the read-only expiration probe "lsuser -a expires tmp_user" against a fixed placeholder account and always renders NOT_ASSESSED, because which accounts are temporary and whether each is removed or disabled within 72 hours is answered only by the onboarding interview. The interview question this check needs is recorded in README.md.

When a bash session ends it should print a logout message so anyone watching the console knows the session is over. If the ~/.bash_logout file for a bash user is missing or prints nothing, the logout is silent and the end of the session goes unannounced.

Checks DISA AIX STIG V-215410 (medium): AIX must boot only from the system boot device. A non-hard-disk device (cd, rmt, ent, network, usb, tok, fddi, or other) in the normal boot list is a finding, and a boot list with no boot device configured is a finding. The SMS firmware multi-boot clause is not visible from the OS, so a hard-disk-only normal boot list still renders NOT_ASSESSED for the manual portion; this check never emits PASS for V-215410.
This check verifies that neither the normal nor service AIX bootlist uses removable media as its boot loader.

This check verifies that AIX CDE conceals the display, via the session lock, within a short window as DISA STIG V-215212 requires. It reads the CDE install state and every dtsession*saverTimeout and dtsession*lockTimeout value in the /etc/dt/config/*/sys.resources site files, failing when a site config file is missing or any timeout exceeds 15 minutes. When CDE (X11) is not used, the control is Not Applicable.

The CDE login greeting must display the DoD banner. This check verifies that the Dtlogin*greeting.labelString resource in /etc/dt/config/en_US/Xresources carries the Standard Mandatory DoD Notice and Consent Banner so users are shown the required notice immediately prior to graphical login; when CDE is not used the rule is Not Applicable.

AIX CDE must provide the xlock command so users can lock their sessions until they reauthenticate. When AIX CDE (X11) is not used the rule text says the control is Not Applicable; when it is in use, the X11.apps.clients fileset and the /usr/bin/X11/xlock binary must both be present, because without xlock an unattended CDE session stays unlocked and exposed to anyone at the console.

This check verifies that the default AIX system accounts (bin, sys, adm, and lpd, with root excepted) are not granted cron access. If /var/adm/cron/cron.allow exists it must not be empty and must not list those accounts; if it does not exist, those accounts must instead be listed in /var/adm/cron/cron.deny. When a default system account can submit cron jobs, those jobs run with the privileges of that account and can be used to maintain unauthorized access or disrupt scheduled work.

This check verifies that every csh/tcsh user has a $HOME/.logout file that displays the STIG logout message when their session ends. A csh/tcsh user who is missing .logout, or whose .logout does not display the message, is not warned that they are being disconnected. The per-user ls/cat commands are templated with the home directory of each subject.

This check verifies that a host using IPv6 has a default IPv6 gateway, unless the host is itself a router. When IPv6 is enabled but no default inet6 route exists, off-link IPv6 traffic has no exit path and cannot be routed reliably; DISA STIG V-215264 requires the default gateway to be configured.

This check verifies that device files (block and character) on local jfs/jfs2 filesystems, and the directories that hold them, are not world-writable except for device nodes the vendor intends any user to open, such as /dev/null. A world-writable device node or a world-writable directory containing device nodes lets any local user replace or remove the node and thereby disrupt or divert the device it represents.

This check verifies the AIX DHCP client (dhcpcd) is disabled: no dhcpcd process runs and /etc/rc.tcpip has no uncommented "start /usr/sbin/dhcpcd" line; a commented-out "#start /usr/sbin/dhcpcd" line is the normal "chrctcp -d dhcpcd" disabled state, not documentation of a needed client. A running DHCP client can silently obtain network configuration from an untrusted DHCP server. DISA STIG V-215355 requires the client disabled, Not Applicable unless needed by the system and documented; recognized only via an operator-written "# PTXRAY-EXEMPT: V-215355 <justification>" marker in /etc/rc.tcpip.

This check verifies that the DHCP daemon dhcprd is not started from /etc/rc.tcpip. When DHCP is not enabled in the network on AIX, an uncommented start line for /usr/sbin/dhcprd would launch the daemon at every boot, exposing an unneeded DHCP server. Any output from the anchored read is the finding; absence of the start line is the compliant state.

This control verifies that the DHCP server daemon (dhcpsd) is not configured to start at boot when the host is not required to serve DHCP. DISA STIG V-215405 states the rule as a prohibition: running the check command must yield no output at all. If a "start /usr/sbin/dhcpsd" line is present in /etc/rc.tcpip, the system boots a service that hands out IP addresses and network configuration, letting a rogue client or an attacker redirect traffic or hand out conflicting addresses.

This check verifies that the AIX DHCP client does not send dynamic DNS updates. When the DHCP client is running, any uncommented "updateDNS" directive in /etc/dhcpc.opt or /etc/dhcpcd.ini causes the client to publish dynamic DNS updates, which can inject uncontrolled records into the DNS namespace. The requirement is Not Applicable when AIX does not run the DHCP client. AIX grep exits 2 when one of the two config files is absent, so a matched line is still a finding and an empty rc=2 result is resolved against a config-file readability probe.

This check verifies that AIX protects information at rest with the Encrypted File System: the clic.rte fileset is installed and the required filesystem reports EFS enabled. Whether the organization requires data-at-rest encryption, and which filesystems are in scope, is a site/ISSO determination the check does not auto-decide; a missing required filesystem, a failed probe, or an unparseable EFS flag refuses with a typed not-assessed.

AIX must encrypt user data at rest using the AIX Encrypted File System (EFS) when the organization requires encryption at rest. EFS needs the clic.rte.lib and clic.rte.kernext filesets and an EFS-enabled jfs2 filesystem; a data filesystem reported as "EFS: no" or a host missing the clic filesets leaves user data at rest unencrypted.

This check verifies that AIX runs with enhanced Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) enabled, so the sys0 enhanced_RBAC attribute is true. Enhanced RBAC isolates security functions from nonsecurity functions, grants system privileges to operating system admins through RBAC roles, and prohibits unprivileged users from installing system software. When enhanced RBAC is off or unconfigured, security functions are not isolated and system privilege is not gated through RBAC.

This check verifies that /etc/security/failedlogin is a real file and not a symbolic link. AIX appends one record per unsuccessful remote login attempt to that file; if the path is a symlink, those records can be redirected to another file or location, so the local audit trail for failed remote logins is lost.

This check verifies the ownership, group, and permission bits of five files mandated by the DISA STIG for IBM AIX 7.x — /etc/inetd.conf, /etc/ntp.conf, /etc/group, /etc/hosts, and /etc/syslog.conf. Any file that exists and is more permissive than the ceiling of its rule, or owned or grouped by the wrong id, fails; an absent file is not applicable. A wrong-owned or over-permissive config file is a documented hardening gap an auditor will flag.

This check verifies that every file and directory on the system has a group that resolves to a valid group. A file or directory whose group does not resolve to a known identity is detached from any accountable group and can be claimed or altered by an unintended group, so its ownership does not meet the STIG requirement.

This check scans the whole local filesystem tree from / for files named .forward. A .forward file silently diverts mail destined for one user to an arbitrary address, so an unintended account or system can collect mail that was never meant for it. Any .forward file anywhere on the system is a finding.

This check verifies that every LDR_PRELOAD list in the global initialization files (/etc/profile, /etc/bashrc, /etc/security/.login, /etc/environment, /etc/security/environ) contains only absolute library paths or $PATH. A relative preload entry lets a process started from those files load a library from the current directory, so an attacker who can drop a library there injects code into any session that sources the file; an empty preload slot is equally invalid.

The check reads the PATH assignments in the global initialization files, the login and non-login shell startup files along with the environment and security files. A finding is any PATH entry that is relative, meaning it does not begin with a slash, or empty, meaning a leading, trailing, or doubled colon. A relative or empty entry lets a shell resolve a command from the current directory or another attacker-writable directory ahead of trusted system directories, so a malicious binary placed there runs with the privileges of the user who invokes the command.

This check verifies that the AIX group database file /etc/group has no extended ACL. An extended ACL on /etc/group adds access rules beyond owner/group/other, so accounts the base mode does not list can be granted read or write access to the group database and alter group membership without the intended administrative control (DISA STIG V-215328).

This check verifies that no interactive account is configured with a blank or null password. An account with a blank password can be signed into without presenting any credential, so any such account is a finding.

This check verifies that every file and directory inside each user home directory is group-owned by a group of which the home directory owner is a member. When a home-directory entry belongs to a group the owner does not belong to, accounts outside the intended set of the owner can reach the entry through the group permission bits, so data of the owner is exposed to unintended group access.

All AIX interactive users home directories must be group-owned by the primary group of the home directory owner (DISA STIG V-215277). A home directory whose group is not the primary group of its owner lets members of the wrong group read or alter the files of the user, so PTxray compares the home directory group id of each interactive user against the primary group id of the user from /etc/passwd and reports any mismatch.

This check verifies that the AIX print-service access files — /etc/hosts.lpd, or the equivalent Systems and printers.conf — contain no line consisting only of a "+" character. A bare "+" grants print access to every host, so an unauthorized host could submit print jobs to the LP subsystem; when none of the three files exists the rule is not applicable.

This check verifies that AIX does not process ICMP timestamp requests: the IPsec filter device is Available (lsdev -Cc ipsec shows ipsec_v4 or ipsec_v6) and the filter table (lsfilt) denies ICMP type 13 (timestamp request) inbound and ICMP type 14 (timestamp reply) outbound. Answering ICMP timestamp requests widens the network attack surface.
The Internet Network News (INN) server must be disabled on AIX: innd/nntpd must not be running, must not be enabled in inetd.conf, and must not be defined in SRC.

Interactive (login-capable) accounts must be assigned a home directory in /etc/passwd and that directory must exist. An account with no home directory, or a home directory that has been removed, breaks login and user state and hides unauthorized access, so every interactive user must have an assigned home directory that is present on the filesystem.

This check verifies that the home directory of every interactive (non-system) AIX user is owned by that user, as required by DISA STIG V-215276. When a home directory belongs to another account, that account can alter the startup files and environment of the user, so the home of every interactive user must be owned by the respective user.

AIX must employ a deny-all, allow-by-exception IPsec default filter so connections to other systems are blocked unless an explicit permit exception exists. This check reads the Rule-ID 0 all-traffic filter rule for IPv4 and IPv6 and verifies its action is deny rather than permit.

This check verifies that the autoconf6 daemon is not started at boot on a server where IPv6 is not utilized. An enabled autoconf6 starts the IPv6 address-autoconfiguration daemon, an unneeded network-facing service on a non-IPv6 server that an auditor will flag; the required state is that no uncommented "start /usr/sbin/autoconf6" line appears in /etc/rc.tcpip.

commands: awk -F: '$7 ~ /(^|\/)(ksh|sh)$/ { print $1 "|" $6; n++ } END { if (n == 0) print "none" }' /etc/passwd
sh -c 'for home in `cut -d: -f6 /etc/passwd`; do if ls -alL $home/.logout >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo "$home|present"; else echo "$home|missing"; fi; done'
sh -c 'for home in `cut -d: -f6 /etc/passwd`; do if cat $home/.logout 2>/dev/null | awk "NF { found=1 } END { exit !found }"; then echo "$home|message"; else echo "$home|empty"; fi; done'
sh -c 'for home in `cut -d: -f6 /etc/passwd`; do if grep "trap '\''\$HOME/.logout'\'' EXIT " $home/.profile >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo "$home"; fi; done'
checks.blurb: Interactive ksh and Bourne users must have a ~/.logout that displays a logout message and a ~/.profile EXIT trap that calls $HOME/.logout.

This check reads the bindpwd and ldapsslkeypwd fields in the AIX LDAP client configuration file /etc/security/ldap/ldap.cfg and flags a finding when a bind or SSL key password is stored in plaintext instead of encrypted or absent. A plaintext directory password is recoverable by anyone who can read the file.

This check verifies that the LDAP client refreshes user and group caches in less than a day. DISA STIG V-215205 requires usercachetimeout and groupcachetimeout in /etc/security/ldap/ldap.cfg to both be present, uncommented, and no greater than 900 seconds; any value above 900 lets the client hold stale user or group entries for a day or more. When LDAP authentication is not required the requirement is Not Applicable.

If the AIX system uses LDAP for authentication or account information, the LDAP SSL/TLS connection must require the server to provide a certificate and that certificate must have a valid path to a trusted CA. This check verifies the decidable sub-condition: LDAP usage, useSSL=yes, and a configured ldapsslkeyf key database. Confirming that the certificate in the key database was issued by DoD PKI or a DoD-approved external PKI requires the KDB password and gsk8capicmd, which is the site/ISSO manual portion.

This check verifies that when LDAP authentication is required (authtype ldap_auth in /etc/security/ldap/ldap.cfg), SSL is used between LDAP clients and LDAP servers (useSSL yes), protecting the integrity of remote access sessions. It reads /etc/security/ldap/ldap.cfg with two read-only greps; LDAP authentication without useSSL yes is a finding.

If the AIX LDAP client is used for authentication (authtype:ldap_auth) it must connect to the LDAP server over SSL. authtype:ldap_auth without useSSL:yes is a finding; when the LDAP client is not used for authentication the requirement does not apply.
LDAP SSL must use only DoD PKI-established certificate authorities to verify protected sessions.

This check verifies that the AIX ldd command is disabled (mode 0000) or absent. An executable ldd can be pointed at an untrusted binary and load or run it, so a mode more permissive than 0000 is a finding.

commands: sh -c 'find /usr/lib/security /usr/lib/methods -type f | while read file; do aclget "$file" 2>/dev/null | grep -e "[[:space:]]enabled$" >/dev/null 2>&1 && printf "%s\n" "$file"; done; printf "scan complete\n"'
checks.blurb: This control verifies that no regular file under the system library directories /usr/lib/security and /usr/lib/methods carries an extended ACL (extended permissions enabled). The STIG inline script writes each aclget dump to a temp file and greps it for a whitespace-prefixed "enabled" line; this read-only port runs aclget to stdout and never writes a temp file. Any library file with an enabled extended ACL can grant principals beyond the intended base permissions access to security-critical library code, so any such file is a finding.

AIX library files under /usr/lib and /lib must have mode 0755 or less permissive. A more permissive mode lets an unprivileged account replace a library used by privileged processes, so the file could be swapped for a hostile implementation.

This check verifies every account has maxulogs set and in 1..10 so concurrent sessions cannot exceed 10. An account with maxulogs unset, 0, or greater than 10 can hold unlimited or excessive simultaneous logins, so a stolen password can be used from many places at once.

This check verifies that the AIX lock command and its supporting bos.rte.security fileset are present. Without /usr/bin/lock a user cannot retain their session lock until reauthenticated, so an unattended session can be left open to walk-up access.

This check verifies that both /usr/bin/lock and /usr/bin/X11/xlock are present so users can directly initiate a session lock for all connection types. When either session lock command is missing, a user cannot lock an unattended session, leaving it open to anyone with physical access to the console.

AIX log files must not have extended ACLs except as needed to support authorized software. This check verifies the decidable sub-condition: aclget of files under /var/log and /var/adm shows extended permissions disabled. Whether every system log file was identified, and whether an enabled ACL is documented with the ISSO as needed for authorized software, is the site/ISSO manual portion.
AIX log files under /var/log and /var/adm must have mode 0640 or less permissive. Log files more permissive than 0640 can leak or be altered.

This check verifies that AIX log files under /var/log, /var/log/syslog, and /var/adm are owned by a system account. A log file owned by some other account can be altered or truncated to hide activity.
