This check verifies that AIX log files under /var/log, /var/log/syslog, and /var/adm are owned by a system group so a non-system group cannot alter or suppress logs. Confirming the system-group policy for the site beyond the authored set remains an ISSO judgement this check does not automate.

This check verifies that a crontab job runs the AIX package management tool lppchk daily to verify installed software, as DISA STIG V-215426 requires. When no such job exists, corrupt or mismatched installed filesets can go unnoticed and the system software is never verified.

This check verifies that no lpd entry exists in /etc/inittab. When the AIX system does not act as a remote print server for other servers, an lpd entry is a finding because the line printer daemon would start and accept remote print jobs, exposing an unnecessary network service.

This check verifies that the piobe print job backend has no /etc/inittab entry. When the system does not support local or remote printing, STIG V-215350 requires the piobe service to be disabled; an inittab entry that init can start leaves an unnecessary print service available. Any output from "lsitab piobe" is a finding.

This check verifies that the AIX qdaemon (the print spooler) is disabled when local or remote printing is not required. A qdaemon entry in /etc/inittab starts the spooler at every boot; DISA STIG V-215348 requires that entry to be absent so printing services do not run unless the site actually needs them.

This check verifies that every AIX global initialization file (/etc/profile, /etc/environment, /etc/security/environ, /etc/security/.profile, /etc/csh.login, /etc/csh.cshrc) contains the "mesg n" (or "mesg -n") command and that none contains the "mesg y" command, so users are denied write access to the terminal and another user cannot write to or capture an active session.
AIX MFA PAM must point TRUSTEDCAS at a real server_ca.pem so the authenticator can verify the MFA server; a missing or unusable CA file means MFA cannot be trusted.
PowerSC MFA (pam_pmfa.conf) TRUSTEDCAS, MFA-URL, SERVER-VERSION=2, and CTC-PROMPT-ONLY=Y configuration.

This check verifies that IBM PowerSC MFA filesets are installed so Multi Factor Authentication is available. When those filesets are missing, the operating system cannot require a second authentication factor.
This check verifies that AIX accepts and verifies Personal Identity Verification (PIV) credentials by having the bos.ahafs fileset installed and the pmfahotplugd subsystem active.

This check verifies that /etc/security/mkuser.sys.custom does not exist. When that overlay is present, every newly created user account is customized by it, which DISA STIG V-215169 treats as a finding unless the overlay is required.
The default primary group for new regular users must be staff (or equivalent) on AIX, so that new accounts are not created in an overly privileged or untracked group.

This check verifies that the shipped /etc/security/mkuser.sys script has not been customized directly. Site customizations must be placed in /etc/security/mkuser.sys.custom; a directly edited mkuser.sys can be overwritten by system updates and bypasses the supported customization contract, breaking or silently altering user account creation.

AIX removable media, remote file systems, and any file system not containing approved device files must be mounted with the nodev option. This check decides NFS and removable-media stanzas in /etc/filesystems; whether a local file system contains approved device files is a site/ISSO judgement and is never auto-passed.

This check verifies that the ndpd-host (IPv6 Neighbor Discovery host) daemon is not started at boot on a system that does not use IPv6. The rule is Not Applicable when ifconfig shows IPv6 (inet6) configured. When IPv6 is not in use, an uncommented "start /usr/sbin/ndpd-host" line in /etc/rc.tcpip is a finding: it boots an unneeded network-facing daemon that an auditor will flag on a non-IPv6 server.

The ndpd-router daemon must not be started from /etc/rc.tcpip. A start command for it at boot brings up the IPv6 router discovery daemon, which DISA STIG V-215368 requires disabled; a matching start line is the finding.

This check verifies the DISA STIG network-option tunables for IBM AIX 7.x: IP forwarding must be off (ipforwarding and ip6forwarding = 0), TCP half-open connection cleanup must be on (clean_partial_conns = 1), and broadcast ping must be off (bcastping = 0). Each tunable is read from "no -a" and compared to its required value; a tunable left at the wrong value is a hardening gap an auditor will flag.
This check verifies that every configured AIX NFS export has an anonymous UID or GID of -1, 60001, 60002, 65534, or 65535, values intended to have no permissions.

This check verifies that every NFS file system is mounted with the nosuid option so setuid programs from an NFS server cannot run with local privilege. NFS mounts that omit nosuid are a finding. Whether a missing nosuid is allowed because the file system contains ISSO-approved setuid or setgid programs remains a typed site review and is never treated as a silent pass.
This check fails when no NIS domain name is configured and refuses (does not PASS) a configured name so site/ISSO can judge whether it is difficult to guess.
This check reads the nosuid mount option on every NFS client mount and reports a finding when a mount lacks it, because a setuid binary on a remote export could then run with local privileges.

This check verifies that the AIX openssl.base fileset is installed at VRMF 20.13.102.1000 or later, the STIG V-215216 floor for NIST FIPS-validated OpenSSL used to provision digital signatures, generate cryptographic hashes, and protect unclassified information requiring confidentiality.

This check verifies that AIX PAM does not enable the rhosts_auth module. When an uncommented rhosts_auth entry is present in /etc/pam.conf, the .rhosts file becomes a supported authentication source, so trust-based rhosts authentication is possible and host equivalence grants can defeat centralized account control.

commands: awk '/^sshd/ { n++; if (n <= 3) print } END { if (n == 0) print "ABSENT" }' /etc/pam.conf
checks.blurb: This check verifies that AIX remote sshd uses the PowerSC PAM MFA stack (pam_ckfile, pam_permission, pam_pmfa). When the first three sshd lines of /etc/pam.conf do not match that stack, remote connections can authenticate without Multi Factor Authentication.

This check verifies that every group identifier (GID) referenced in /etc/passwd field 4 is defined by a group in /etc/group field 3. A GID without a matching group entry means the owning account resolves to an undefined group, which breaks ownership, permissions, and access control across the system.
This check verifies that every passwd.nntp file on jfs/jfs2 has mode 0600 or less permissive. When no such file exists, NNTP is treated as not in use.

This check verifies that every login shell in /etc/passwd is listed in /etc/shells or the login.cfg usw shells list, except shells used to prevent logins. Required AIX shells must appear in that allowed set. An unlisted login shell lets an account run a shell the administrator did not authorize.

This check looks for a plus character in /etc/passwd, /etc/security/passwd, and /etc/group. A plus without defined NIS+ or LDAP netgroup entries lets network-defined users and groups take part in local authentication. Mid-line pluses and /etc/security/passwd are in scope.

This check verifies AIX rate-limits half-open TCP connections on network interfaces by requiring bos.net.tcp.client_core to be COMMITTED and clean_partial_conns to be 1, limiting Denial of Service effects from incomplete connection floods.

This check verifies that every public directory — a world-writable directory with the sticky bit set — is owned by root or a site-approved application account. When a public directory belongs to another account, that account controls the files any user may write there, can tamper with or delete them, and can hide their actions, so the STIG requires the owner to be root or an application account.
LDR_PRELOAD lists in control scripts must contain only absolute paths (or $PATH) with no empty colon entries.

This check verifies that AIX run control scripts under /etc/rc* set LIBPATH with only absolute directory entries (the $PATH variable is accepted because it expands to absolute directories). An empty entry (leading, trailing, or doubled colon) or an entry that is not an absolute path lets the dynamic loader search an unintended directory, which can load a substituted library at boot or service start.
Run-control executable search paths must contain only absolute entries: no empty PATH slots and no relative components such as . or bin.

This check verifies that /usr/bin/rcp, /usr/bin/rlogin, /usr/bin/rsh, /usr/bin/rexec and /usr/bin/telnet are mode 0000 (----------) or absent. Those programs are the legacy rcmd and telnet clients; if they remain executable a user on this host can start a cleartext remote login or remote command that exposes credentials and session data.

This check verifies that the Reliable Datagram Sockets (RDS) protocol is not loaded on the system. RDS is a kernel-level datagram transport loaded as a kernel extension; DISA requires it to be disabled because it is not needed for normal operation and adds to the local attack surface. Any RDS line in the loaded kernel extension list is a finding.

This check verifies that Group Identifiers reserved for AIX system accounts (GIDs 0 through 99) are not assigned as the primary group of a non-system account. A non-system login that inherits a reserved GID shares the group identity of system accounts and can read or alter group-owned system files those GIDs protect.

This check verifies that UIDs reserved for system accounts (0-128) are not assigned to non-system accounts on AIX. A regular user account holding a reserved UID inherits the privileges and identification reserved for system accounts, so every reserved-UID occupant must be a recognized AIX system account.

Administrative accounts must not run a web browser except as needed for local service administration. This partial-automation check identifies root browser profile directories and leaves authorization intent to the root users and ISSO.

AIX root LDR_PRELOAD list must be empty. STIG check-content greps the env output for LDR_PRELOAD in the root shell of the auditor; this scanner reads /etc/environment, /.profile, and the profile of root instead.

commands: sh -c 'last() { command last | head -n 200; }; last | grep "root " | egrep -v "reboot|console" | more'
checks.blurb: root passwords must never travel the network in clear text; a non-console root login with sshd down is the finding.

This check verifies the root account password field in /etc/passwd is locked ("!"). AIX must require authentication when booting into single-user and maintenance modes; an unlocked root password field lets a walk-up attacker boot into a maintenance shell without a password, which violates DISA STIG V-215308.

This check reads the executable search path of the root account and lists the permissions of each directory on that path. A finding is a world-writable directory on the path. A world-writable directory allows an unprivileged writer to plant a namesake binary that root later executes.

This check verifies that the rlogin attribute for the root account is false. With rlogin enabled, the root account can log in directly over the network through rlogin, bypassing the requirement that root log in only from the system console.

This check verifies that the AIX root user home directory is not the root directory (/). When the root user logs in with the root directory as home, commands and files behave unexpectedly and root-owned data is exposed at the top of the filesystem, so the home directory must be a dedicated directory such as /root.

This check verifies that the home directory of the root account has no extended ACL. An extended ACL on that directory grants rights to principals the base permissions do not list, widening the root environment boundary, so DISA STIG V-215199 requires the directory carry base permissions only.

This check verifies that AIX is not running routing protocol daemons (ospfd, bgpd, zebra, quagga, gated, routed). The STIG allows an exception when the host is a designated router; that role is a site decision and is not auto-detected.
This check verifies that Samba packages are absent from AIX, as required by DISA STIG V-215280.

This check verifies that Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) is not installed on the AIX host. SCTP support is carried by the bos.net.sctp fileset; when that fileset is installed, SCTP endpoints and transports can be created, expanding the attack surface without an operational need. When lslpp does not list the fileset, SCTP is absent and the host passes this STIG control.

commands: lssec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a loginretries -a maxulogs -a minupperalpha -a minloweralpha -a mindigit -a mindiff -a minage -a maxage -a minlen -a minspecialchar -a maxrepeats
checks.blurb: This check measures the AIX account and password-policy attributes in /etc/security against the DISA STIG for IBM AIX 7.x: login retry and logging limits, password length, character-class mix, reuse distance, minimum/maximum age, and login delay. Any attribute weaker than its mandated value fails, because it is a documented hardening gap an auditor will flag and it applies to every account inheriting the default stanza. The check only reads these attributes; it never changes them.

AIX must set the Stack Execution Disable (SED) system-wide mode to all. A system-wide SED mode other than all is a finding; a determinate absence of the SED subject is the compliant state (prohibition convention), never a refusal.

This check verifies that the SMTP service HELP command is not enabled. sendmail serves the HELP command when the O HelpFile option in /etc/mail/sendmail.cf names a help text file that exists on the system. When that option is absent, the subject sendmail.cf is absent, or the named help file is missing, the HELP command is not enabled. The HELP command discloses the sendmail command grammar to connecting peers.
This check verifies that sendmail LogLevel in /etc/mail/sendmail.cf is not set below 9, so mail activity is logged at STIG depth.

This check verifies that sendmail is absent or new enough that the DEBUG SMTP command is not implemented. Sendmail versions below 8.6 still implement DEBUG. Evidence is the bos.net.tcp.sendmail fileset level from lslpp, not an invocation of the MTA binary.

If this AIX server does not host an SNMP agent, the dpid2 daemon must not be started from /etc/rc.tcpip. An uncommented start /usr/sbin/dpid2 boot entry is the decidable sub-condition; whether the host hosts an SNMP agent is a site/ISSO determination, so a matching start line is not assessed as a failure until that premise is answered.

This check verifies that named is not started from /etc/rc.tcpip unless the host is a DNS server. A start /usr/sbin/named line at boot enables an unneeded name-server daemon on hosts that are not DNS servers.
If this AIX server is not a multicast router, mrouted must not be started from /etc/rc.tcpip. An uncommented start /usr/sbin/mrouted line boots a multicast routing daemon the host does not need.

This check verifies that the SSH daemon terminates idle sessions within ten minutes. STIG V-215290 requires ClientAliveInterval of 600 seconds or less and ClientAliveCountMax of 0 in /etc/ssh/sshd_config. When those settings are missing or looser, an unattended SSH session stays open for reuse.

This check verifies that the AIX SSH daemon does not allow compression when OpenSSH is older than 7.4. Compression on those versions can leak data from encrypted SSH sessions; OpenSSH 7.4 and above make the requirement not applicable.

This check verifies that the AIX SSH daemon is configured to reject empty passwords. PermitEmptyPasswords yes, or a missing uncommented directive, lets an account with no password authenticate over SSH.

This check verifies that the AIX SSH daemon is configured to ignore user .rhosts files (IgnoreRhosts yes). When that directive is missing or is not yes, SSH can honor per-user .rhosts trust and allow host-based login that bypasses the system authentication policy.

The AIX SSH daemon must be configured to use only Message Authentication Codes (MACs) that employ FIPS 140-2 approved cryptographic hash algorithms. Any other MAC, an empty MAC list, or a missing MACs setting is a finding.

commands: sh -c "test -r /etc/ssh/sshd_config || exit 1; grep -i StrictModes /etc/ssh/sshd_config | grep -v '^#' || echo STRICTMODES_ABSENT"
checks.blurb: This check verifies that the SSH daemon performs StrictModes checking of home-directory configuration files so unauthorized users cannot plant or alter those files to hijack sessions.
This check verifies that SSH uses /etc/motd.ssh to display the complete Standard Mandatory DoD Notice and Consent Banner for SSH, sftp, and scp login sessions.

This check verifies that the SSH daemon disables GSSAPIAuthentication when GSSAPI authentication is not required. The SA or ISSO must confirm whether GSSAPI is used for SSH authentication; PTxray reports that manual portion as not assessed when it is not supplied.
This check verifies that the AIX SSH daemon is explicitly configured not to use host-based authentication.
This check verifies that private SSH host key files are no more permissive than mode 0600. A group- or world-readable private host key can let another user impersonate this host.
This check verifies that sshd configuration does not enable KerberosAuthentication, so Kerberos authentication cannot bypass the system access restrictions.

This check verifies that the SSH daemon listens only on approved IP addresses. When ListenAddress is missing or binds all interfaces, the daemon accepts connections on every address; whether a specific non-loopback bind is ISSO-permitted needs site policy and is not silently passed.

This check verifies that the SSH daemon has privilege separation turned on. Privilege separation prevents the SSH daemon from remaining fully privileged after authentication, so a compromised session cannot act with the original privileges of the daemon.

This check verifies that the AIX SSH server uses SSH Protocol 2 only. An absent Protocol directive is accepted only when sshd reports OpenSSH 7.4 or later, because those releases removed the directive and support Protocol 2 only.

The check reads the RevokedKeys setting in /etc/ssh/sshd_config. A finding is raised when that setting is missing, empty, or unset, so revoked public keys are not disabled. That matters because a revoked key that was stolen or compromised keeps working, letting an attacker authenticate.

This check verifies that the SSH daemon does not allow RhostsRSAAuthentication. That obsolete OpenSSH 7.4 directive trusts rhosts plus RSA host keys, which weakens SSH authentication. If any uncommented setting is yes, this is a finding; absence or a syntactically valid non-yes value is the compliant prohibition state. A matching directive with no parseable value is not assessed.

commands: sh -c "[ -r /etc/ssh/sshd_config ] || exit 2; grep -i AllowTcpForwarding /etc/ssh/sshd_config | grep -v '^#'; STF_PRC=\$?; if [ \$STF_PRC -eq 1 ]; then printf '%s\n' ptxray_absent_allowtcpforwarding; exit 0; fi; exit \$STF_PRC"
checks.blurb: This check verifies that the SSH daemon has TCP forwarding turned off. TCP forwarding lets an authenticated SSH session relay TCP connections through the host, so a session that should only provide a shell can reach other network services.

This check verifies that the AIX SSH daemon is configured for IP filtering through TCP wrappers. OpenSSH 6.7 and later do not use TCP wrappers, so the requirement does not apply on those releases. On older OpenSSH, missing sshd entries in /etc/hosts.allow and /etc/hosts.deny leave the daemon unfiltered by source address.

This check verifies that the SSH daemon has reverse name checking turned on. Reverse name checking stops SSH from trusting a client whose claimed hostname does not match a reverse lookup of its address. VerifyReverseMapping is obsolete in modern OpenSSH (UseDNS replaced it); this check still evaluates the STIG directive literally.

commands: sh -c 'X11F_GREP=$(grep -i X11Forwarding /etc/ssh/sshd_config); X11F_GREP_RC=$?; if [ "$X11F_GREP_RC" -ne 0 ]; then exit "$X11F_GREP_RC"; fi; printf "%s\n" "$X11F_GREP" | grep -v "^#"'
checks.blurb: This check verifies that the SSH daemon has X11 forwarding turned off. When X11Forwarding is missing or set to yes, graphical sessions can be tunneled through SSH.

commands: sh -c '_out=$(lslpp -i) || exit $?; printf "%s\n" "$_out" |grep -i ssh || echo "openssh.base.server not installed"'
checks.blurb: This check verifies that AIX runs the SSH server for replay-resistant authentication to privileged and non-privileged accounts. openssh.base.server must be installed and the sshd subsystem must be active.

This check verifies that OpenSSH server is installed and sshd is active so AIX can protect the confidentiality and integrity of transmitted information and so non-encryption network access methods stay disabled.

This check verifies that AIX sudoers configuration does not use the !authenticate option. That option lets a sudo command run without re-authenticating the invoking user, so a stolen session can keep using elevated rights. Hosts that do not use sudo are not applicable.

This check verifies that sudoers configuration files do not contain a NOPASSWD tag. A NOPASSWD grant lets a user run privileged commands without re-authentication, so a compromised account can escalate without leaving a password prompt in the audit trail.

This check confirms that the legacy network services the DISA STIG for IBM AIX 7.x requires disabled are actually off: no inetd service token is left enabled in /etc/inetd.conf, and no daemon is left set to start at boot in /etc/rc.tcpip. Any still-enabled or boot-started service is an unneeded, often unauthenticated, network-facing daemon an auditor will flag. If the service inventory cannot be read, the check reports NOT_ASSESSED instead of guessing.

This check verifies that system command directories do not have extended ACLs. An extended ACL on /etc, /bin, /usr/bin, /usr/lbin, /usr/ucb, /sbin, or /usr/sbin lets a non-owner change or replace those files.

Kernel core dumps must be disabled unless needed. On a managed AIX system a dump device is needed, so a configured dump device is NOT_APPLICABLE citing V-215407; this check never FAILs a real dump device.
system files/programs/directories not group-owned by a system group can be modified by that group.

This check verifies that system files, programs, and directories under /etc, /bin, /usr/bin, /usr/lbin, /usr/ucb, /sbin, and /usr/sbin are owned by a system account (authored as UID 0-128 per V-215195, plus ipsec). An unauthorized owner can replace those programs or configuration files.

This check verifies that the AIX syslogd daemon does not accept remote messages unless the host is a syslog server documented using site-defined procedures. A running syslogd without the -R flag accepts network log traffic that can flood logs or hide local events.
AIX must log TCPD events via syslogd with an uncommented mail. selector in /etc/syslog.conf. When that selector is missing, or the file itself is absent, TCPD is not logging.

AIX must send syslog to a documented remote log host. An uncommented action token beginning with @ in /etc/syslog.conf is the decidable part; whether that host is justified and documented is a site/ISSO question this check does not silently pass.
This check verifies that TCP wrappers hosts.allow and hosts.deny exist and that hosts.deny contains ALL:ALL so hosts not listed in hosts.allow are denied.

This check verifies that AIX employs strong authenticators for nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions by confirming the telnet subserver is not active. An active telnet subserver accepts cleartext credentials for remote maintenance.

This check verifies Trusted Execution Check policy has TE, CHKEXEC, and CHKKERNEXT all ON. When any of those attributes is OFF, the kernel will run unverified executables or kernel extensions, so a modified or planted binary can execute.

This check verifies that AIX authenticates through PAM: the usw stanza auth_type in /etc/security/login.cfg must be PAM_AUTH so multi-factor authentication can be configured. Any other value, or a missing auth_type subject, is a finding.

This check verifies that every user core dump size is 0 so process cores cannot leak memory contents. An account with core unset or set to a nonzero size can write process memory to disk, exposing credentials and other in-memory data.

This check verifies that the default stanza and every user have a non-empty dictionlist so AIX rejects dictionary-word passwords. An empty dictionlist on default or any account lets users choose common words as passwords.

This check verifies that the default login herald displays the Standard Mandatory DoD Notice and Consent Banner before access. When the herald is unset or omits that notice, a publicly reachable login proceeds without the required warning and consent text.

This check verifies that AIX user home directories do not have extended ACLs (DISA STIG V-215332). An extended ACL on a home directory lets a non-owner change or replace files belonging to that account.

This check verifies that the default stanza and every user have loginretries set between 1 and 3 so AIX locks an account after three consecutive invalid logins. A value of 0 or greater than 3 on default or any account leaves the account unlocked after repeated failed passwords, so an attacker can keep guessing.

This check verifies that the default stanza and every account have maxage set between 1 and 8 weeks so passwords cannot live longer than 60 days. An unset, 0, or greater-than-8 maxage on default or any account leaves a password valid indefinitely or well past that lifetime.

This check verifies that default and every account have maxrepeats set to 1, 2, or 3 so AIX rejects passwords with more than three consecutive repeating characters. An unset, 0, or greater-than-3 value on default or any user disables that limit and lets guessable runs of the same character through.

This check verifies that the /etc/security/user default stanza and every account have minage set to at least 1 so a password cannot be changed within 24 hours. A missing or sub-1 default, or any account with minage less than 1, lets a newly set password be replaced immediately.

This check verifies that AIX requires password changes to replace at least 50 percent of characters. Default and every account must have mindiff set to 8 or greater; an unset or weaker mindiff lets a user keep most of an old password.

This check verifies that the default stanza and every user require at least one numeric character in passwords (mindigit >= 1). An unset or zero mindigit on default or any account lets users choose passwords with no digits.

This check verifies that the default stanza and every account enforce minlen of at least 15 so short passwords are rejected. An unset minlen, a default below 15, or any user below 15 lets accounts choose passwords shorter than the STIG requires.

This check verifies that AIX password complexity requires at least one lower-case character. The default minloweralpha value in /etc/security/user must be set to 1 or more, and minloweralpha for every account must be 1 or more. An unset or weaker value lets users choose passwords with no lower-case letters.

This check verifies that AIX requires at least one special character in passwords. The default stanza and every account must have minspecialchar set to 1 or more; a value of 0 or an unset value lets users choose passwords with no special characters.
AIX must require at least one upper-case character in passwords (minupperalpha >= 1 on the default stanza and every account).

This check verifies that AIX password hashes were generated with a FIPS 140-2 approved algorithm (ssha256 or ssha512): pwd_algorithm is one of those values, /etc/passwd field 2 contains no hashes, and every hash in /etc/security/passwd begins with {ssha256} or {ssha512}.

Direct logins must not be permitted to shared, default, application, or utility accounts. This check reads the rlogin attribute for the default AIX accounts (adm, bin, daemon, guest, lpd, nobody, nuucp, sys, uucp). If any of those accounts has rlogin=true, that account can be reached over the network. Shared, application, and utility accounts are named by the ISSO/ISSM and are not decided here.

This check verifies that /etc/shells exists and that the login.cfg usw shells attribute is a non-empty subset of it (V-215408). A missing file or empty shells attribute is unmet required configuration. Whether a listed shell is ISSO-approved is site judgement and is never silently passed.

The AIX SYSTEM attribute must not be NONE for any account (V-215177). SYSTEM=NONE on any account is a finding: that account is not authenticated by any method, so a login is accepted without a credential.

This check verifies that the /etc/security/user default stanza and every interactive account have ttys=ALL so users can log in on any terminal. A missing or non-ALL default, or any interactive account without ttys=ALL, leaves a required login path blocked or narrowed.

This check verifies that AIX sets default file-creation permissions so authenticated users can only read and modify their own files. /etc/security/.profile must contain umask 077 and the /etc/security/user default stanza must have umask=077; a looser or unset umask lets new files be group- or world-readable.

Local initialization files must list only absolute paths in LDR_PRELOAD. A relative or empty colon slot can load an attacker-controlled library into the processes of a user. Paths that are absolute still require ISSO/ISSM authorization, which this check cannot decide.

Local init-file library search paths must contain only absolute entries. Relative paths, empty colon slots, and a missing required init file are findings. History files are not init files and are not scanned.

This check verifies that every interactive AIX user home directory has mode 0750 or less permissive. A more permissive home lets another identity read or alter the files of the account. Unclassified passwd homes are assessed against 0750. Application directories are allowed 0755 or less permissive.

This check verifies that every account name on the AIX host is unique by reading usrck -n ALL (report mode, no changes). Duplicate names break accountability because one name maps to more than one account record.

This check verifies that /usr/sbin/wall is present so administrators can send a message to currently logged-in users. When that command is missing, there is no supported way to warn those users of a system event.

Public directories must be the only world-writable directories, and world-writable files must live only in public directories (V-215409). World-writable objects outside /tmp and /dev/null are a finding; whether additional objects are required for system or application operation is an ISSO judgement and is never a silent PASS.
AIX must keep /usr/bin/write present so admins can send a message to a currently logged-in user.

This check verifies that /var/adm/wtmp is a real login accounting file rather than a symlink. When that path is a symlink, successful remote logins can be redirected or suppressed so they are not recorded for monitoring.

This control inventories the physical storage layout, recording each disk, its volume group, size, and SAN path count. That inventory exists to be checked against the approved storage topology so a disk in the wrong place or missing redundant paths would be caught. If the check cannot be completed, such misplacement or missing redundancy can go unnoticed, and a single disk or path failure could then cause an outage or data loss.

This control checks where sudo writes a record of the commands it runs. It verifies that sudo is still logging to the system log, or to its own dedicated log file, rather than silently dropping those records. If sudo logging is turned off with no alternate file in place, privileged commands can run with no record left behind, allowing an attacker who has gained access to operate without an audit trail.

This check verifies that sudo is configured with the use_pty option, which makes every command run through sudo execute inside its own separate terminal. When that option is missing or explicitly disabled, a program run through sudo shares the terminal of the user who launched it and can inject keystrokes into that session, allowing a compromised program to take over an administrator session.

This check confirms that the sudo command installed on the host reports a release at or above the required patched baseline. An older release may still carry published security flaws, which can allow an attacker to escalate from a limited account to full administrator control of the system.

This control inventories every setuid and setgid program on the system and confirms each one is authorized. A setuid or setgid program runs with the privileges of its owner, usually root, no matter who starts it. An unauthorized one can let any user run commands as root, so a planted or unapproved program of this kind hands an attacker full control of the system.

This control scans for symbolic links that point to files or directories that no longer exist on local JFS/JFS2 filesystems. A dangling link is not harmless leftover clutter: the empty path it names can later be claimed by another user or program, so anything that follows the link can be silently redirected to unexpected content. If this control fails, a link that used to point at a trusted file could be made to point at something an attacker placed there.

This control verifies that the server has a real system dump device configured so that a crash can be captured for later diagnosis. If the primary dump device is unset or disabled, a system panic produces no dump at all, and the cause of the outage must be guessed rather than determined from evidence.

This control checks that the syslogd logging daemon is running with the -r option, which makes it accept incoming log messages sent from other systems. If it is running without that option, log messages from other computers are silently discarded, so break-in attempts or misuse on those systems never reach the central log.

This check confirms that the syslog configuration has at least one active logging rule and that the log files it is expected to write to exist on disk. If it fails, the system may not be recording events at all. An attacker could then act without leaving a trace of failed logins or other suspicious activity, and operators would have no log trail to investigate a breach or diagnose an outage.

This check verifies that the system is configured to forward log entries to a remote log server rather than keeping the record only on the machine itself. If no remote destination is set, an attacker who gains access can delete or rewrite the local logs to erase evidence, and a disk or system failure can destroy the only copy of the record.

commands: lsuser -a login rlogin shell account_locked ALL
checks.blurb: The adm account is a built-in AIX account used for system administration and accounting, and it is not meant for people to log into. This check confirms the account is either absent or fully locked down, with local and remote login disabled, a non-working shell, and the account locked. If it can still be logged into, an attacker who takes it over gains a foothold with access to that administrative and accounting data, which could be read or altered.

commands: lsuser -a login rlogin shell account_locked ALL
checks.blurb: This check confirms the built-in bin account cannot be used to sign in to the system. It passes when the account is absent or locked, with local login, remote login, and command-shell access all turned off. If the account stays open, bin owns many trusted system programs, so an attacker who logs in as bin gains an interactive shell and a direct way to alter those files.

commands: lsuser -a login rlogin shell account_locked ALL
checks.blurb: The daemon account is a built-in AIX system account that runs background services and should never be able to accept a login. This control verifies the account is locked, has no usable login shell, and allows no remote login. If it is left able to log in, an attacker who obtains its credentials gains an interactive foothold on the system and access to the files that identity owns.

commands: lsuser -a login rlogin shell account_locked ALL
checks.blurb: This control checks that the built-in guest account is either absent from the system or fully locked down, with local and remote login disabled, a non-working shell, and the account itself locked. If the guest account can still be used to log in, an attacker gains an easy, well-known foothold on the system from which to explore and escalate.

commands: lsuser -a login rlogin shell account_locked ALL
checks.blurb: The lpd account exists only to run the line printer service and should never be able to log in interactively. This control confirms the account is either removed entirely or locked with all of its local, remote, and shell login paths disabled. If it fails, the lpd account can still be used to sign in, giving whoever holds it a working entry point into the system.

commands: lsuser -a login rlogin shell account_locked ALL
checks.blurb: The nobody account is a well-known, built-in account that ships with AIX and is meant to have no way to log in. This control checks that the account is either not present or fully locked down with every login path disabled. If it still allows a login, an attacker can sign in as nobody and use that known account as a foothold to run commands and work toward higher access.

commands: lsuser -a login rlogin shell account_locked ALL
checks.blurb: This control checks that the legacy nuucp system account is either removed or fully locked down by disabling its local login, remote login, and login shell, and by locking the account itself. The nuucp account exists on AIX for the obsolete UUCP file-transfer service, and a well-known default account like this is a common first target for attackers. If the account is left active with a usable login path, an attacker could log in under that identity and use it as a foothold to move deeper into the system.

commands: lsuser -a login rlogin shell account_locked ALL
checks.blurb: The sys account is a built-in AIX system account that owns system files and is not meant for anyone to sign in to. This check confirms the account is absent, or that it is locked with its local login, remote login, and login shell all disabled. If any of those login paths is left open, an attacker who obtains the account gains an interactive foothold on the system and access to the files that identity owns.

commands: lsuser -a login rlogin shell account_locked ALL
checks.blurb: This check confirms the uucp system account has every login path closed and is locked. The uucp account belongs to a legacy file-transfer service and is not meant for anyone to sign in to. If it keeps a usable local or remote login path, an attacker who takes it over can use this trusted system account to move or alter transferred files and hide their activity.

This check confirms that the built-in system accounts, including root, are listed in /etc/ftpusers, the file that blocks those accounts from signing in over FTP. If any of them are missing, an attacker could sign in over FTP as root or another system account on any system where an FTP service is running, and FTP sends passwords in clear text. That could give an attacker full control of the system or a way to act as a trusted service account.

This control checks that address-space layout randomization is running at full strength on the system. ASLR loads each program and its data at unpredictable memory locations, so an attacker who finds a memory-corruption flaw in software cannot reliably predict where to redirect execution. If this protection is weak or disabled, memory addresses become predictable and an attacker can more easily turn such a flaw into the ability to run their own code on the system.

This control checks that the system is set up to record its own hardware and software configuration on a regular schedule, and that its inventory log is saved to a local file. If either of these is missing, there is no dependable record of how the system was set up, so changes from an outage or an intruder can go unnoticed and are hard to reconstruct afterward.

Trusted Execution enforces that only programs approved in the system trust database are allowed to run, so a modified or planted executable is blocked before it starts. This check also confirms that the system records those enforcement events in its syslog. If it fails, tampered or malicious code can run, and the log of what was blocked or allowed is lost.

This control checks whether the AIX Trusted Execution subsystem has its kernel policy lock enabled, the LOCK_KERN_POLICIES setting. When the lock is on, the kernel enforces the security policies it loaded at boot and refuses any attempt to change or replace them while the system is running. If the lock is off, someone with administrator-level access could swap out or unload an active security policy at runtime, weakening the protections the system was configured to enforce.

This control verifies that Trusted Execution is configured to block programs that have not been approved. If these settings are off, the system will run executables that were never validated, so an attacker who places an unapproved program on the server could run it and execute malware or unauthorized code.

Trusted Execution checks each program against a database of trusted signatures before it runs, and Trusted Execution Path limits the directories the system searches when launching programs. If either protection is off, a modified or malicious program can run without being verified, and a planted binary can be substituted for a trusted one.

This control compares every installed file against the trusted signature database of the operating system to confirm that nothing has been altered, replaced, or added without authorization. When a file fails that comparison, it means software on the system has been tampered with or an unauthorized program has been installed, giving an attacker a hidden foothold and possible privileged access.

Trusted Execution (TE) makes AIX check the integrity of every program before it runs, so a tampered or malicious binary is refused. When TE is off, the kernel runs any executable without that check, and an attacker who can place a modified binary can run it without detection. DISA STIG V-215335 requires TE to be enabled.

This check reads the file of kernel settings that AIX will apply at the next reboot. It flags any non-default values so each change can be reviewed and justified. Unreviewed kernel tuning can alter memory, network, or storage behavior in ways that surprise operators or hurt performance.

This check confirms the system timezone (TZ) is set explicitly in /etc/environment, so logs, scheduled jobs, and timestamps reflect the correct local time. If it is unset, the system may record ambiguous local times, which can confuse audit trails and make incident review unreliable.

This control checks that root is the only account with UID 0, the special number that gives an account full control over the machine. If any other account also has UID 0, every one of those accounts can act as the administrator. That means a single compromised password among them lets an attacker take over the whole system.

This control checks the default umask value in /etc/security/user, the AIX file that holds user settings. That value controls the permissions automatically given to every new file and directory a user creates. If it is missing or too permissive, new files and directories can be created readable or writable by other users on the system, exposing data or letting others change it.

This check scans the whole local filesystem tree from / for any file or directory whose numeric owner no longer resolves to a known account. When an account is removed, the files it owned are left behind with an unresolvable owner: no one is accountable for them, they escape normal access review and cleanup, and a later account that reuses the same numeric ID silently takes ownership of them. Any such file or directory is a finding.

This control measures how much free space is left in each active volume group, the storage pools that filesystems draw from when they need to grow. If any volume group falls below five percent free, there is no headroom to enlarge a filesystem when it fills up, so applications and users can be blocked from writing data at the moment storage is needed most.

This check looks at whether a VIOS configuration backup is current. It runs viosbr -autobackup status and viosbr -view -list. Node or cluster configuration changes that are Complete pass. An empty backup directory warns only when status is not already current. It does not read crontab, and it does not run backupios or viosbr -backup. A plain AIX LPAR is not applicable. ck-backup-job stays pared.

This check reads the VIOS level with ioscli ioslevel and grades it against the existing EOS_VIOS currency table. A confirmed non-VIOS LPAR is not applicable. An unreadable level is not assessed. The check never changes the VIOS level.

This check inspects the Shared Ethernet Adapter of a VIOS and CAA cluster state to infer whether the box is a single point of failure. A failover-ready SEA (ha_mode auto, standby, or sharing, plus a control channel) or a CAA cluster implies a partner VIOS and passes; a SEA that cannot fail over, with no cluster to replace it, fails; when no SEA and no cluster are visible the check reports not-applicable; and a failed SEA probe is not assessed. This check emits only vios_topology.

commands: lsuser -a shell account_locked login rlogin ALL
checks.blurb: This check inventories login-capable Virtual I/O Server accounts other than the factory padmin user. IBM ships a VIOS with only padmin active; an extra login expands who can reach the appliance. On a plain AIX partition the VIOS user model does not apply.

commands: lsuser -a shell account_locked login rlogin ALL
checks.blurb: This check confirms that login-capable accounts on a Virtual I/O Server use the ioscli restricted shell. IBM VIOS lsuser documents those accounts as using the rksh shell; a ksh, sh, bash, or oem_setup_env login shell skips that wrapper and is the persistent form of oem_setup_env unrestricted AIX access. On a plain AIX partition the restricted-shell model does not apply.

This check reads the VIOS viosecure firewall page and nothing else. IPv4 Firewall OFF is a warning: a factory VIOS is not a pass and is not a failure for a firewall that was never enabled. IPv4 Firewall ON with an allowed-ports table passes. No address on the host is not an input. A plain AIX LPAR is not applicable.

This check reads whether a VIOS has a viosecure hardening level applied. It runs only the read-only view. A factory page that says security rules are not applied is a warning, not a pass. A page that names an lls, mls, or hls rule is an applied level. A plain AIX LPAR is not applicable.

Checks that the AIX Virtual Memory Manager file-cache thresholds (minperm, maxperm and maxclient) are at their default values and that the file cache is not pinned at its ceiling. When these thresholds are wrong for the workload, the partition either re-reads the same data from disk repeatedly, or cached files evict the pages running programs need, making the system slower than it should be.

This check reads vNIC server adapters with ioscli lsmap -all -vnic. The name token is vnicserver plus an instance number. No vnicserver row is not applicable, including on a VIOS that has a Shared Ethernet Adapter. One or more rows pass. A failed command is not assessed. vnicstat -r is not run.

This check reads the Backing device token from ioscli lsmap -all, the same capture as vscsi_maps. Every token shaped hdisk plus digits passes. The viosupgrade checklist (https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/node/6258119) does not print a logical-volume name shape, so any other non-empty token is not assessed. No vhost is not applicable. It does not re-grade a missing or Defined virtual target, and it does not run viosbr.

This check verifies that every virtual SCSI host adapter (vhost) on a VIOS has a live backing device, so the client LPARs mapped to them are actually being served their vSCSI disks. A vhost with no virtual target device, or a target left "Status Defined" (offline), means a client LPAR disk is not being served — usually left behind by a rebuild or a failed backing hdisk.

This check confirms every vSCSI backing LUN on a VIOS is free of SCSI reservation (reserve_policy no_reserve), so dual-VIOS vSCSI failover can actually work. A reserved backing LUN fails silently: everything looks mapped and dual, but the partner VIOS cannot open the LUN and the disk of the client never comes back on failover.

This check looks in /etc and /usr/local/bin for files that any user can write to. A file that anyone can modify is a risk because an ordinary user could change system settings or replace a program with a hostile copy. Finding such a file means the system is open to that kind of tampering.

This check finds shared directories that every user can write to but that are missing the sticky bit, the setting that keeps users from deleting or renaming files they do not own. Without that protection, any local user can remove or replace files belonging to other users, which can disrupt running services and may be used to run a program as another account.

This control checks whether any regular file on a local JFS or JFS2 filesystem is world-writable, meaning any user on the system can change it. If such files exist, anyone with an account could modify or replace programs, scripts, and configuration files, which can lead to tampering with system behavior or unauthorized access.

This check looks for non-directory objects on local filesystems that are writable by their group and owned by an administrative group. If that group-write access has not been reviewed and approved, any member of the group, or anyone who compromises one, can change those files. That can allow tampering with programs or configuration to take control of the system.

This check confirms the writesrv write server is not running. writesrv is a network service that lets someone, including a user on another machine, push a message straight onto the screen of a logged-in user through the write command. If it is left active, that service is an unnecessary opening on the machine, and it can be used to send spam or spoof messages that interrupt a user or trick them into trusting a fake sender.
